opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think tool use is one of the most practical levers we have right now. When you look at where LLMs tend to fail, a lot of it comes down to things the model was never really designed to do well inside its weights. Exact arithmetic, looking up current information, recalling a specific fact that appeared maybe once or twice in the training data. The model is essentially trying to compress all of that into parameters, and it ends up guessing or hallucinating something that sounds plausible.

With tool use, you let the model offload those parts. If it needs to compute something, it can call a calculator or run a bit of Python. If it needs a fact, it can query a search engine or a database. The model then focuses on what it's actually good at, which is understanding the question, breaking it down, deciding what information it needs, and then synthesizing an answer from the results.

There's also a nice side effect for smaller models. You don't necessarily need a gigantic model that memorizes the whole world if it can reliably look things up. That makes things cheaper to run and easier to keep current, because you're not retraining every time the world changes.

And from a trust perspective, it helps too. If the answer is grounded in a tool output, say a retrieved document or the result of a code execution, you can trace where it came from and verify it. That's much harder when everything comes out of the model's internal knowledge.

Of course, it's not free. The model has to learn when to call a tool, which tool, and how to handle bad or irrelevant results. That's a training and evaluation challenge in itself. But overall, I see it as a very promising direction, probably complementary to reasoning improvements, rather than competing with them.

r001.rationale: The response says an LLM can use a calculator or Python for computation, but does not compare that to a human using a calculator.

r002.rationale: It explains that tool use lets the model offload tasks where it would otherwise guess or hallucinate, and that tool outputs can ground and verify answers.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the core issue is that a language model, at the end of the day, is a next-token predictor trained on a static snapshot of text. It's really good at producing fluent, plausible-sounding output, but "plausible" and "correct" are not the same thing. If you ask it to multiply two large numbers, or tell you what happened last week, or compute some statistic from a dataset, it has no mechanism to actually verify what it's saying. It's essentially recalling patterns from training, and when the pattern isn't there, it will still produce something confident-sounding, which is where hallucinations come from.

Tool use is attractive to me because it addresses that at the root rather than trying to patch it. Instead of asking the model to be a calculator, a search engine, a database, and a Python interpreter all at once, you let the model do what it's actually good at, which is understanding the request and deciding what needs to happen, and then you offload the parts that require precision or up-to-date information to systems that are designed for that. So the model writes the code and the code gets executed. The model formulates the query and a retrieval system returns the actual documents. The answer is then grounded in something real rather than in the model's internal approximation of reality.

And there's a second aspect that I find really important, which is scaling. We've been getting better models mostly by making them bigger and training them on more data, but that's expensive and it has diminishing returns for certain kinds of tasks. You can make a model ten times larger and it will still be unreliable at arithmetic. But a model that can call a calculator is perfectly reliable at arithmetic, regardless of size. So tool use gives you a way to extend capabilities without having to bake everything into the weights. In my experience, a smaller model with good tool access can often outperform a much larger model that's working from memory alone, and that's a much more efficient path.

I'd also add that it changes the failure mode in a healthy way. When a tool-using model gets something wrong, you can often trace it: the search returned the wrong document, the code had a bug, the API returned an error. That's debuggable. Whereas when a pure language model is wrong, it's just wrong somewhere inside billions of parameters, and there's not much you can do except retrain. So from an engineering standpoint, I think tool use makes these systems more transparent and more maintainable, not just more accurate.

r001.rationale: The response says a model can call a calculator for arithmetic, but it does not compare that to a human using a calculator.

r002.rationale: It links tool use to grounding answers in external results and says this addresses the source of hallucinations.

astra-6.text:
I think tool use is important because we don’t have to expect the language model to do everything itself. If you ask it to do a calculation, it might produce something that looks plausible, but a calculator is much better suited to that task. The model can recognize that it needs a calculation, call the tool, and then explain the result.

The same idea applies to information. Instead of relying entirely on what it learned during training, it can retrieve relevant information and use that to answer the question. That’s especially useful when the information changes over time.

Of course, calling a tool doesn’t automatically make an answer correct. The model still has to choose the right tool, provide the right inputs, and interpret the output. But it gives us a way to improve answers beyond just making the model bigger: let the model coordinate tasks and use specialized tools where they’re more reliable.

r001.rationale: The response says an LLM can use a calculator for calculations, but does not compare this to a human using one for difficult arithmetic.

r002.rationale: It describes retrieval and other ways tools can improve answers, but does not state that tool use can reduce hallucinations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the key things is that we don’t have to expect the language model to do everything internally. If you ask it to do a calculation, for example, it might produce a plausible answer, but a calculator is a much more reliable tool for that particular task. The model can figure out what needs to be calculated, call the tool, and then explain the result.

The same idea applies to looking up information. Instead of relying entirely on what’s stored in its parameters, the model can retrieve relevant information and use that to answer the question. So you’re combining the language model’s ability to interpret a request and communicate with tools that are better suited to specific parts of the problem. Of course, it still has to choose the right tool and interpret the output correctly, but that gives us a practical way to improve answers without putting every capability into the model itself.

r001.rationale: It says an LLM can use a calculator for a calculation, but does not compare this to a human using one for difficult arithmetic.

r002.rationale: It describes retrieving information instead of relying only on model parameters, but does not state that tool use reduces hallucinations.
